abstract.gco:CharacterString: OverviewOcean Chemistry variables are provided on a ~10 km grid covering the Australian region for global warming levels +1.2 °C, +1.5 °C, +2.0 °C, +3.0 °C and +4.0 °C. Data are derived from atmospheric fields from CMIP5 RCP8.5 global climate model data used to drive an eddy-resolving model (Ocean Forecasting Australian Model version 3, OFAM3). The data is based on just one realisation of the future ocean state.Rising atmospheric CO2 levels increase the uptake of CO2 by the oceans. About 28% of anthropogenic CO2 emissions since 1800 have been absorbed by the oceans. This affects the oceans’ carbonate chemistry and decreases their pH, a process known as ocean acidification. The pH changes in surface waters are primarily driven by increasing CO2 in the atmosphere, causing the uptake of CO2 which reacts with water producing hydrogen ions and a pH decrease.Data are available for global warming levels +1.2 °C, +1.5 °C, +2.0 °C, +3.0 °C and +4.0 °C (with respect to the pre-industrial 1850–1900 mean value), created using data from an ocean model simulation. The data is based on just one realisation of the future ocean state.The datasets in this collection show a single realisation for ocean hydrochemistry variables. The data were used in Australia’s National Climate Risk Assessment (2025).Indices includedSurface pH – mean annual surface pH for the Australia region in the current climate, and the change in pH mean state at each GWL.Note: This dataset is not visualised on the ACS Hazard Data Explorer.Technical detailsThe data consists of gridded data covering the Australian region in NetCDF format. Data are provided for global warming levels +1.2 °C, +1.5 °C, +2.0 °C and +3.0 °C, and were created using bias-adjusted output from climate model simulations.Global warming levels represent 20-year periods where the average global temperature reaches +1.2 °C, +1.5 °C, +2.0 °C and +3.0 °C above the global average temperature for the pre-industrial period (1850–1900). Global warming level +1.2 °C is sometimes referred to as the “current” climate as it covers 2011–2030.The National Climate Risk Assessment used ~10 km resolution ocean modelling driven by atmospheric data from CMIP5 (~10 km resolution ocean modelling driven by data from CMIP6 was not available). The data used in the assessment comes from a future ocean simulation which uses the multi-model mean from CMIP5 atmospheric forcing fields under the RCP8.5 projection to drive an ocean eddy-resolving model (Ocean Forecasting Australia Model version 3, OFAM3). Data are provided globally, and collected into separate datasets for the global warming levels for the Australian Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) and marine subregions.Observations and modelling of ocean warming and acidification are limited by the short timescales of global ocean surface and deep ocean observations fit for model use, as well as our understanding of the global ocean circulation. Impacts from and to the high latitudes, including ice sheet loss and sea ice changes, are critical to a global understanding.It is important to note the CMIP type global models have nominal resolution of about 1 degree (~100 km in the Australian region). CMIP models can represent large scale changes in the open ocean (e.g. meridional overturning circulation) but lack the resolution to represent the boundary currents around Australia (e.g. East Australian Current, Leeuwin Current) which are critical to future changes in the ocean arounds Australia.In the open ocean, CMIP simulations do represent the large-scale future changes in ocean acidification. However, CMIP models under-estimate ocean acidification variability in the continental shelf regions of Australia.The downscaled product used in this data collection, with resolution of about 10 km, is suitable for representing these boundary currents and the changes in the ocean regions around Australia. However, in the coastal regions (water depth less than 100 m), a resolution of 1 km is needed to represent local circulation features and how they will respond to future change, which is important to issues like the existence of refugia for coral bleaching.To prepare the data for publishing the ACS has applied consistent land, sea and data void masks.Supporting documentsA technical report that describes the creation of the data:Jakob D, Risbey J, Bahramian K, Bende-Michl U, Benger N, Bhardwaj J, Black M, Bongiovanni K, Bourbon H, Buchanan P, Carrara E, Do C, Evans A, Fox-Hughes P, Gregory R, Griesser A, Grose M, Hague B, Hoffmann D, Howard E, Irving D, Jacobs S, Jones D, Maguire S, Matear R, Narsey S, O’Grady J, Oke A, Osbrough S, Parker T, Pepler A, Peter J, Rafter T, Ramsay H, Rogers C, Sharples W, Stassen C, Stellema A, Su C-H, Takbash A, Thatcher M, Tolhurst G, Tozer C, Udy D, Watkins A and Zhang X (2025) Climate Hazard Information developed for use in Climate Risk Assessment, Bureau Research Report, Australian Bureau of Meteorology.A technical report that provides supporting technical material used to assess the implications of climate change on marine natural ecosystems:Bugnot AB, Woolley S, Brodie S, Bustamante RH, Dunstan P, Richardson AJ, Blanchard J, Blamey L and Fulton E (2025) Natural Ecosystems Technical Report: Marine.
